Konskie Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Końskie, Poland

Demolished. Końskie's Jewish presence is first documented in 1588, growing to comprise over half the town's population by 1827 and reaching 5,037 people (60.8 percent) by 1921. This cemetery, most likely established in the second half of the 17th century, also served Jews from several outlying villages, including Czarna, Stąporków, Krasna, and Wąsosz. During WWII, the Germans destroyed the cemetery, using its tombstones to pave a street, build a swine feed yard, and construct a tower in Modliszewice; broken tombstones were also sold to residents for construction. In 2008, plans to build a bypass road directly through the cemetery grounds were modified only after the personal intervention of Rabbi Michael Schudrich, the Chief Rabbi of Poland; recovered tombstones continue to be brought back to the site, and in 2017 local government allocated land to build a dedicated lapidarium for them.
